newsitem.title: MAURITANIA: Mauritanians vote for new national assembly.
newsitem.headline: Mauritanians vote for new national assembly.

text.p: Nicholas Phythian
Mauritanians voted on Friday for a new national assembly, with opposition candidates and women seeking seats for the first time in a major test of the West African nation's fledgling democracy.

Polling in Nouakchott, the dusty capital of the mainly Moslem former French colony, began slowly and in many areas poll organisers, party representatives and voters highlighted problems with voting cards.
Opposition supporters, many of whom expressed irritation at the heavy turnout of soldiers and other members of the security forces at polling stations, cried fraud.

Returning officers and supporters of President Maaouya Ould Sid'Ahmed Taya and the ruling Democratic and Social Republican Party blamed administrative inadequacies -- problems such as mistyped identity card numbers on the voter lists.
"It's a problem for everyone," Taya supporter Bilal Saleh said at the town hall in Ksar, a ruling party stronghold.

Ould Sid Ahmad Khattar, a 29-year-old businessman standing as an independent on a youth party ticket in one of the area's polling stations, disagreed. "There is fraud going on. My supporters have not been able to vote," he said.
Polling was slow during the morning. Voters -- the men in blue or white robes, the women in brightly coloured muslin -- squatted in the sand, waiting patiently in separate queues.
Soldiers and security forces guarded polling stations, checking voters' credentials before allowing them in.
By noon little more than a quarter of eligible voters seemed to have cast their ballot in many polling stations.
Almost half the 2.2 million people in the impoverished nation at the Atlantic fringe of the Sahara Desert are eligible to vote. Polls opened at 7 a.m. and close at 7 p.m.
It was not immediately clear how the poll was going in the interior of the sparsely population country.
Taya and the ruling party emerged victorious from 1992 elections that launched Mauritania's multi-party experiment. The ruling party won 67 of the assembly's 79 seats.

The opposition, which boycotted the 1992 poll denouncing irregularities, is hoping to make its mark ahead of a presidential election due by January 1998. It has accused the authorities of censorship, denying it a fair hearing this time.

Dominant light-skinned Moors of Arab stock and blacks each make up a third of the population in the arid, former French colony which won independence in 1960. Arabic-speaking ex-slaves make up the remainder.
The government formally banned slavery in 1980.
Taya, a French-trained army colonel, seized power in a bloodless coup in 1984. He launched the democratic transition in 1991 and won a six-year term as president a year later.
Thirteen political parties have put up candidates for Friday's poll along with more than 50 independents -- mostly disgruntled ruling party members passed over for the poll.
Most of the 26 women candidates are from the ruling party.
First results are expected on Friday night but the final results could take a couple of days to emerge. Second-round run- offs are planned for October 18.
